solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Benefits, eating nothing but mushrooms (8)

indicatorNotes.eating: something that eats takes food inside itself, so the outer word swallows the other

annotation.surface: Someone lives on benefits and eats nothing but mushrooms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mushrooms' reads as a food, but it is the verb: costs that mushroom are growing fast.
annotation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe something swelling suddenly and rapidly, like costs or debts getting out of hand.

entries.clue: Doctor’s vehicle pinched by abject pervert (10)

indicatorNotes.pinched by: to pinch is to squeeze between finger and thumb, so the vehicle is gripped between two outer letters

blocks.note: the TARDIS is Doctor Who's time machine

annotation.surface: A doctor's car gets nicked by some low-life deviant.
annotation.walkthrough: The Doctor is Doctor Who, whose police-box time machine is the TARDIS; 'pervert' is a verb here, not the person in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean corrupting something, debasing it from its proper or original form.

entries.clue: Fatigue over, monkey around (7)

indicatorNotes.around: around means encircling, so the monkey's letters surround the abbreviation for over

blocks.note: the langur is an Asian monkey
o = over, the cricket scoring abbreviation

annotation.surface: Tiredness is over, so it's time to monkey around.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Monkey around' reads as a phrasal verb; split, the monkey is a noun and 'around' places it.
annotation.definitionFit: The word names a weary, listless lack of energy, the heavy tiredness of a hot afternoon.

entries.clue: Piece trimmed from wrong allocation (6)

annotation.surface: A piece has been unfairly cut from someone's share.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a grievance about a short share; 'allocation' and 'wrong' only pretend to belong to it.
annotation.definitionFit: Carpenters and tailors use the word for the leftover scrap sliced away from timber or fabric.

entries.clue: They keep hands nice and secure on ships (4,8)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down answer one word placed on another sits above it, so the first piece stands on top

annotation.surface: Crew who keep their hands tidy and fasten things down on board ship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hands' suggests sailors, which is why the ships feel natural; here they are just hands with fingernails.
annotation.definitionFit: The tool trims fingernails, which keeps hands looking neat and groomed.

entries.clue: Clear leader for campaign in a desert (6)

indicatorNotes.leader for: the leader of a word is the letter at its front, so only its first letter is used
indicatorNotes.in: in places one thing inside another, so the letter goes inside the phrase that follows

annotation.surface: A campaign's leader is cleared of deserting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Desert' is the verb to quit, not sand; and 'Clear' is a legal verdict.
annotation.definitionFit: A court that finds a defendant not guilty clears them of the charge.

entries.clue: Stan’s partner’s whine about mine (8)

indicatorNotes.about: about means surrounding on all sides, so the whine wraps round the partner

blocks.note: Ollie (Oliver Hardy) was Stan Laurel's comedy partner

annotation.surface: Stan Laurel's partner moans about something of mine.
annotation.walkthrough: Laurel and Hardy were Stan and Ollie; 'mine' looks like a possessive but is a pit.
annotation.definitionFit: The word names a coal pit together with its surface buildings and workings.

entries.clue: Taken out by a Parisian of indeterminate age (7)

blocks.note: taken out on a date = dated

annotation.surface: Someone of uncertain age is taken out by a Parisian.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By' puts the French word beside the other piece; here it goes in front, though the clue names it second.
annotation.definitionFit: A document or object carrying no date leaves its age impossible to fix.

entries.clue: Drawn like a bow (4)

blocks.note: a ribbon or shoelace bow is knotted

annotation.surface: A bow drawn back, as an archer does.
annotation.walkthrough: The archer's bow is drawn; the ribbon bow is knotted. A drawn game is also level.
annotation.definitionFit: A match ending level is drawn, and a bow in ribbon or laces is knotted that way.

entries.clue: Small pub arranged fine party (4,4)

indicatorNotes.arranged: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters of the next word are reordered

blocks.note: s = small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A little pub put on a fine party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' reads as a celebration but is a political party, the Irish republican one.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the Irish republican political party, active in both Ireland and Northern Ireland.

entries.clue: Page border split by large word (6)

indicatorNotes.split by: a thing split by a wedge is forced apart, so the size letter pushes between page and border

blocks.note: l = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A page margin interrupted by a big word, as in typesetting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Word' means a promise, as in 'you have my word'.
annotation.definitionFit: Giving your word is making a solemn promise, so the two are the same undertaking.

entries.clue: Hold onto a criminal picked up secretly (6-6)

indicatorNotes.picked up: a radio picks up a signal, so what follows is the sound heard, not the spelling

blocks.note: to hug is to clasp tightly; a mugger is a street robber

annotation.surface: Someone grabs a criminal who was arrested in secret.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' reads as arrested, which suits the criminal, but it means heard. Said quickly, the phrase runs together into the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: The old reduplicated phrase means in concealment, clandestinely, done on the quiet.

entries.clue: I treat those suffering with pins and needles (13)

annotation.definition: I treat those suffering with pins and needles

blocks.note: not the tingling complaint but the tools: the therapy is given with needles

annotation.surface: A doctor who treats the tingling feeling called pins and needles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pins and needles' seems to be the complaint, but it is the treatment: 'with' means using, not suffering from.
annotation.definitionFit: This therapist inserts fine needles into the skin to treat patients, the Chinese medical practice.

entries.clue: Untroubled about one wearing Nazi unit’s uniform (10)

indicatorNotes.about: about means surrounding, so the calm word goes all round the rest
indicatorNotes.wearing: a wearer has clothes wrapped round them, so the Nazi unit wraps round the numeral

blocks.note: the SS, a Nazi paramilitary force

annotation.surface: Someone is unbothered by a man in a Nazi uniform.
annotation.walkthrough: Two containers nest, one inside the other. 'Uniform' is an adjective, not clothing, though the surface dresses it up as clothing.
annotation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe something that never varies, the same throughout.

entries.clue: Nip and tuck (4)

blocks.note: to nip to the shops = to dash there quickly
in dressmaking, a tapered fold stitched in to shape a garment

annotation.surface: Nip and tuck: cosmetic surgery.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as plastic surgery; split, it is a quick dash and a dressmaker's fold.
annotation.definitionFit: The word is a quick sudden movement and also a tapered fold sewn into a garment.

entries.clue: Music producer made good spinning awful discs (10)

indicatorNotes.spinning: a spinning thing turns round, so the word for awful is turned round too

blocks.note: O is disc-shaped, so two discs are OO

annotation.surface: A record producer succeeded by spinning terrible records.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Made good' reads as one phrase meaning succeeded; it splits in two. The producer is an instrument, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the long Aboriginal Australian wooden wind instrument, so it produces music.

entries.clue: Biscuit covering small bowl (8)

blocks.note: in lawn bowls, the jack is the small target ball

annotation.surface: A biscuit covers a small bowl.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' looks like a dish but is the game's small white ball.
annotation.definitionFit: In Britain the word means a chewy baked oat bar, loosely a biscuit; Americans use it for a pancake.

entries.clue: Misery left after war returns (10)

indicatorNotes.after: after means following, so the word for left is placed behind the war's gains

blocks.note: the spoils of war are what it returns

annotation.surface: Misery is what remains once war comes back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Misery' is a person here, as in 'don't be such a misery'; 'returns' means gains, not coming back.
annotation.definitionFit: In British slang a misery is a gloomy killjoy who ruins others' fun.

entries.clue: Secure arms to support old belief (7)

indicatorNotes.to support: a support holds something up from below, so in this down answer the arms go underneath

blocks.note: to pinion someone is to secure their arms

annotation.surface: Guaranteed weapons shore up an old-fashioned faith.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arms' reads as weapons, but it is the limbs held fast.
annotation.definitionFit: Both nouns name a view a person holds to be true, without needing proof.

entries.clue: Wit which Hardy has, but not Laurel (4)

blocks.note: count a certain letter in HARDY: there are none
the letter is U, which LAUREL contains; Hardy has none of those U's

annotation.surface: Hardy had the brains of the famous comedy duo, Laurel never did.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks about the comics' brains; the clue asks about the letters in their names, and 'no U's' runs together as one word.
annotation.definitionFit: The Greek-derived word means practical intelligence, common sense.

entries.clue: Stone fruit in slices (7)

indicatorNotes.slices: a knife that slices cuts into something, so the little word cuts into the fruit

annotation.surface: Stone fruit cut into slices, like a sliced peach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stone fruit' reads as one thing, a plum or a peach; the break falls after 'Stone'.
annotation.definitionFit: It is a green silicate mineral whose gem form, peridot, is cut as a precious stone.

entries.clue: Somebody generous with syrup (6)

blocks.note: Cockney rhyming slang: syrup of figs = wig

annotation.surface: Someone pours syrup freely.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'somebody' is an important person. 'Syrup' is British rhyming slang, from syrup of figs, for a hairpiece.
annotation.definitionFit: A somebody is a person of importance, and the informal word names such a VIP.

entries.clue: Bring in games after university solicitations (13)

indicatorNotes.after: after means following, so the games come behind the university abbreviation

blocks.note: to import is to bring in
a tie is a match, as in a cup tie

annotation.surface: Games are brought in after university, alongside requests.
annotation.walkthrough: A tie is a knockout match in British sport, such as an FA Cup tie.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words name persistent, pressing requests made to someone.

entries.clue: Flipping insect bite! (4)

indicatorNotes.Flipping: to flip something is to turn it over, so the insect's letters run the other way

annotation.surface: An exasperated 'flipping insect bite!'
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is a mild British swear word in the surface; in the wordplay it turns the insect over.
annotation.definitionFit: A sharp, piquant flavour gives food bite, as lemon or vinegar does.

entries.clue: Savage hit during Ali’s first round (6)

indicatorNotes.first: first picks out the opening letter of the boxer's name only
indicatorNotes.round: to turn round is to face the other way, so the whole assembled string is read backwards

annotation.surface: A brutal punch lands during Muhammad Ali's first round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'During' looks like a container instruction but is a plain word, and 'round' is a reversal, not a boxing round.
annotation.definitionFit: A savage is a brutish, uncivilised person, the same sense as calling someone a beast.

entries.clue: Some may be beaten, say, eg with whisks (3,5)

indicatorNotes.whisks: whisking stirs ingredients vigorously, so the letters beside it are mixed up

annotation.surface: Some things get beaten, for example with whisks.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue sounds like a kitchen note, and it describes the answer too: this is exactly what a cook whisks.
annotation.definitionFit: Cooks beat the clear part of eggs into stiff peaks for meringue and souffles.

entries.clue: Health food supplements dislodging kohlrabi (6)

annotation.definitionNote: plural in the clue, singular answer: the tree's extract is sold as supplements
annotation.surface: Health supplements push kohlrabi off the menu.
annotation.walkthrough: There is no separate indicator: the answer simply sits across the two words. Kohlrabi is a turnip-like cabbage.
annotation.definitionFit: Extract from the leaves of this Chinese tree is sold in capsules as a memory-boosting supplement.

entries.clue: Piece of paper cut by inferior paper workers (8)

indicatorNotes.cut by: a thing cut by a knife is split in two, so the first paper is split round the others

blocks.note: the FT, the Financial Times newspaper
a rag is a low-grade newspaper

annotation.surface: A sheet of paper sliced by poorly paid paper workers.
annotation.walkthrough: Both papers are newspapers: the FT is the Financial Times, and a rag is a trashy one.
annotation.definitionFit: Both nouns mean a small part broken or detached from a larger whole.
